FULL-ARCH IMPLANT TREATMENT

This is one of the largest decisions in dentistry, and much of it cannot be undone. Removing the remaining teeth in an arch and
reshaping the bone is permanent. Please read this form, or ask us to read it to you, and do not sign until every question has been answered.
You may change your mind and stop at any point before surgery begins.

2. WHAT “ALL-ON-X” MEANS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN
•
The “X” is not fixed. It is the number of implants needed to support the bridge. The final number, position and angle are decided during surgery,
once your surgeon can see and feel the bone. Fewer or more implants than planned may be placed.
•
Same-day teeth are temporary teeth. If your implants are stable enough on the day of surgery, a temporary fixed bridge is attached. It is made
of acrylic or printed resin, it is not the final result, and it is expected to chip, stain, wear or break during the months of healing. The final bridge is
made later and will look and feel different.
•
This is a prosthesis, not a set of new natural teeth. The bridge is a device that is screwed onto implants. It does not feel, chew or age like
natural teeth. It requires daily cleaning under the bridge, professional maintenance, and eventual repair and replacement.
•
What is removed cannot be put back. Extraction of the remaining teeth and reduction of the jaw bone are permanent. If this treatment fails, the
options remaining to me may be fewer and more difficult than the ones I have today, and a conventional denture on a reduced ridge may fit
poorly.
Longevity, in plain numbers. Implants often last a long time; the bridge on top of them does not last as long. In published follow-up studies of
full-arch fixed prostheses, essentially every prosthesis needed at least one repair by about six years, and roughly 4 out of 5 prostheses were
still in service at 5 years and about 3 out of 5 at 10 years. These figures come from studies of other patients and are not a promise about my
own result. Replacement of a worn or fractured bridge is additional treatment at additional cost.

CONSENT FOR FULL-ARCH IMPLANT TREATMENT (ALL-ON-X)
Patient: ______________________________
3. RISKS OF THE SURGERY
No surgery is risk-free, and no result can be promised or guaranteed. This list cannot include every possible complication.
•
Common, and usually temporary: considerable pain, swelling and bruising of the face and neck for several days — usually more than after a
simple extraction; bleeding and oozing for the first day; stiff jaw and limited mouth opening; sore throat; cracked corners of the mouth; bruising
that can track down the neck and chest; difficulty eating for weeks.
•
Less common: infection needing antibiotics, drainage or a second procedure; wound opening and slow healing; damage to the lips, cheeks,
tongue or corners of the mouth; jaw joint (TMJ) pain, clicking or locking; hematoma; scarring; small pieces of bone that work their way out later;
allergic or other adverse reaction to a medicine or material.
•
Uncommon, but serious: nerve injury — numbness, tingling, burning or pain of the lower lip, chin, gums or tongue, and/or a change or loss of
taste. The lower jaw carries the higher risk, and bone reduction brings the surgery closer to the nerve. This usually improves over weeks to
months, but it can last longer and in some cases is permanent; an opening between the mouth and the sinus or nose; fracture of a thin, atrophic
lower jaw, which may require hospital treatment and plating; infection spreading into the face or neck; heavy bleeding.
•
Rare: medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) — bone that will not heal and stays exposed; the risk is higher with
bone-strengthening or anti-cancer drugs (alendronate, zoledronic acid, denosumab and similar) or previous radiation to the jaws; permanent
change in facial appearance; life-threatening complications.
If zygomatic, pterygoid or trans-sinus implants are used, these additional risks apply:
•
sinus infection or long-term sinusitis, sometimes needing ENT treatment or removal of the implant; oro-antral communication; nasal congestion
or discharge;
•
injury to the infraorbital nerve causing numbness of the cheek, side of the nose or upper lip;
•
penetration into the orbit (eye socket) or, very rarely, injury to the eye or its contents; bruising around the eye; temporary double vision;
•
these implants are technically difficult to remove if they fail, and removal is a larger operation.
4. RISKS SPECIFIC TO FULL-ARCH IMPLANT TREATMENT
•
Not enough stability on the day. If the implants are not firm enough to carry a bridge immediately, same-day fixed teeth will not be
delivered. I will wear a removable temporary denture, which sits on the healing gums and is often uncomfortable, for several months.
•
Implant failure. One or more implants can fail to fuse with the bone, or can fail later. Depending on which implant and when, this may mean
additional surgery, additional implants, grafting, a remake of the bridge, a return to a removable denture, or — if enough implants fail — loss of
the whole plan.
•
Bone reduction is permanent. Reshaping the ridge lowers it and changes its form. A denture made before surgery will not fit afterwards, and a
conventional denture on a reduced ridge is usually less stable than it was before.
•
Speech and adaptation. Most people develop a lisp or altered speech at first and adapt over weeks. Some do not fully adapt. Air or saliva may
escape at the sides. The bulk of the bridge and its position may change how I sound.
•
Cleaning and food trapping. There is a space under the bridge, and food and air pass under it. Cleaning requires a water flosser, superfloss or
threaders, every day, for life. The bridge must be unscrewed and professionally cleaned periodically, which is a separate appointment and fee.
•
Gum and bone changes. Peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis (inflammation with bone loss) can develop around the implants. Gums
shrink over time, which may expose the metal, the junction between the bridge and the gum, or dark spaces — a particular concern if I have a
high smile line. This junction may be visible when I smile or speak.
•
Prosthesis and hardware problems. Chipping and wear of the teeth; fracture of the bridge or its framework; loosening or fracture of screws
and abutments; staining of the access holes; a screw or fragment that is difficult to retrieve. Grinding and clenching (bruxism) sharply
increases all of these, and a protective night guard is usually required — and is my responsibility to wear.
•
Bite, joint and opposing arch. The bite and the vertical height of my face may be changed on purpose. This can affect the jaw joints and
muscles. A hard bridge chewing against natural teeth or another prosthesis can wear or damage the opposing arch, which may then also need
treatment.
•
Appearance. The shape, size, color and lip support of the final bridge are limited by the position of my implants, the bone and the space
available. The result may not match the appearance I imagined, and there are limits to how much it can be changed once the implants are
placed.
•
Systemic and habit factors. Smoking or vaping, uncontrolled diabetes, bruxism, steroids or drugs that lower immunity, previous radiation, and
poor hygiene all significantly increase the chance of infection, bone loss and failure of this treatment.
•
Imaging. Implants and frameworks cause scatter on CT and MRI images. I should tell any future doctor or imaging center that I have them.

I understand that this treatment is a lifelong commitment, not a one-time procedure. If I do not keep my maintenance appointments,
clean under the bridge daily, and wear a night guard if one is prescribed, my risk of bone loss, hardware fracture and failure rises sharply, and

anesthesia

•
All anesthesia, including local: allergic or adverse reaction to a drug; pain, swelling, bruising or lasting numbness where an injection or IV is
placed; nerve injury from an injection; nausea and vomiting; dizziness, confusion, poor coordination or grogginess that can last into the next day;
being aware of parts of the procedure.
•
Sedation and general anesthesia also carry: trouble with breathing or the airway; low blood pressure or an irregular heartbeat; stomach
contents entering the lungs; sore throat, hoarseness, or injury to teeth, lips or gums if a breathing tube or airway device is used; and — rarely —
heart attack, stroke, brain injury, or death.
If you are having any sedation or general anesthesia, initial each line:
I have had nothing to eat or drink for at least 6 hours (clear liquids only up to the time I was told). I understand that eating or
drinking before sedation can be life-threatening.
I have told this office about every medicine and supplement I take, including blood thinners, bone-strengthening drugs, steroids, herbal
products, and any GLP-1 medicine such as semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy), tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) or liraglutide — these
can keep food in the stomach and change the fasting instructions I need.
I took my usual prescribed medicines exactly as instructed, with small sips of water.
A responsible adult is with me today, will drive me home, and will stay with me until I have recovered.
For 24 hours I will not drive, operate machinery or power tools, drink alcohol, be the only adult caring for a child, or sign legal or
financial documents. I understand the medicines may not fully wear off for a day.
I am not pregnant, or I have told the office that I may be pregnant or am breastfeeding.
7. MEDICINES AND PAIN CONTROL
Most oral surgery pain is controlled best by alternating ibuprofen and acetaminophen on a schedule, not by opioids. If an opioid is prescribed
for you, we have discussed the following:
•
It is for short-term use only. New York limits an initial opioid prescription for acute pain to a 7-day supply.
•
Opioids cause drowsiness, constipation, nausea and slowed breathing, and can lead to dependence, addiction and overdose — the danger is
much higher when combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxants, sleep aids or other sedatives.
•
Do not drive or work while taking them.
•
Keep them locked away from children, teenagers, visitors and pets, and take what you do not use to a drug take-back site. Never share them.
•
Naloxone (Narcan) reverses an overdose, is available without a prescription, and may be recommended for your home.
•
Antibiotics can cause upset stomach, diarrhea, C. difficile infection, yeast infection, rash or a serious allergic reaction, and may make hormonal
birth control less reliable.
Opioid risks discussed
No opioid planned
Patient declines opioids
History of substance use disorder
disclosed
8. MY PART IN THE RESULT
•
I have given a complete and accurate medical and dental history, including all conditions, all prescription and non-prescription medicines and
supplements, allergies, recreational drug use and pregnancy, and I will report any change before surgery.
•
I will follow the soft diet I am given — typically nothing hard, crunchy or chewy for the first 8 to 12 weeks. Biting into hard food with a temporary
bridge is the most common cause of early failure.
•
I have been told that smoking and vaping significantly increase the risk that these implants and this bridge will fail, and I have been advised to
stop.

•
I will call the office promptly about pain, swelling, a loose or clicking bridge, bleeding gums around the implants, or a broken tooth on the bridge,

•
I understand that if I do not do these things I am much more likely to have a complication or lose the result, and that corrective treatment may be

9. WHAT I UNDERSTAND AND AGREE TO
•
Dentistry and surgery are not exact sciences. No one has promised or guaranteed me a particular result, an exact appearance, a treatment
length, or how long this will last.
•
Once surgery has begun, my surgeon may find bone or anatomy that was not visible on the examination, x-rays or CT scan. I authorize my
surgeon to change the number, position, angle or type of implants, to add grafting, to withhold the same-day bridge, or to stop the
procedure, if in their professional judgment that is medically reasonable and in my best interest — including while I am sedated and cannot be
asked.
•
I may need more visits, more tests, referral to another specialist, further surgery, or hospital care.
•
Surgical fees, anesthesia fees and prosthetic fees are separate, and additional or corrective treatment may cost more. Insurance may cover little
or none of this treatment.
•
Records, images, scans and models made in the course of my care are part of my dental record and are kept by the practice; I may request
copies.
•
I may withdraw this consent and stop treatment at any time before surgery begins.
Initial each of the following:
I understand that my remaining teeth in this arch will be removed permanently and that bone will be reshaped, and that this cannot
be reversed.
I understand that the teeth placed on the day of surgery are temporary, and that the final bridge is made months later and will look and
feel different.
I understand that the bridge is a device that will require daily cleaning, regular professional maintenance, repair, and eventual
replacement at additional cost.
I understand that implants can fail, that a failure may require more surgery or a return to a removable denture, and that no one has
guaranteed me otherwise.
10. PHOTOGRAPHS, IMAGES AND RECORDS — optional; initial only what you agree to
Photographs, video, x-rays, scans and models may be taken and used for my own diagnosis, treatment planning and dental
record. (Required in order to provide care.)
They may also be used without my name for teaching, professional lectures, study clubs and publication in professional literature.
They may also be used without my name on the practice website, in advertising and on social media. I understand that once an
image is published online it may be copied and may not be possible to withdraw completely. I may revoke this in writing for future use

2. WHY THIS IS BEING PROPOSED, AND WHAT ELSE I COULD DO
A custom subperiosteal implant is a titanium framework that is made from a scan of my own jaw and rests on the bone underneath the gum,
with posts that come through the gum to hold a bridge. It is normally proposed when there is not enough bone for ordinary implants and when
grafting is not possible, has already failed, or has been declined.

3. WHAT IS KNOWN — AND NOT KNOWN — ABOUT THIS DEVICE
My surgeon has told me plainly that this device does not have the long-term track record that ordinary dental implants have, and has
explained the following:
•
History. Subperiosteal implants were used from the 1940s and were largely abandoned by the 1990s because too many of them failed over the
long term, usually by becoming exposed and infected. Today's version is a redesign — planned from a CT scan and 3D-printed to fit my jaw —
but it is the same basic idea, and it has not yet been followed for as many years as the old one was.

CONSENT FOR A PATIENT-SPECIFIC / SUBPERIOSTEAL IMPLANT
Patient: ______________________________
•
How strong the evidence is. The published studies are small, are mostly case series without a comparison group, and include no randomized
trials. Reviewers have rated the overall certainty of this evidence as very low. Roughly one study in five reports results beyond three years, and
about one in ten beyond five years.
•
What those studies report. In the short and medium term, most of these implants stay in place — reported survival is roughly 70% to 100%,
with an average follow-up of under two years in the largest review. Complications of the gum over the framework are common: part of the
framework becoming exposed through the gum has been reported in about 1 in 4 patients overall, and in some series in as many as 2 out of 3.
Persistent soft-tissue infection was reported in about 1 in 20.
•
What this means for me. My surgeon cannot tell me how long this device will last, cannot promise it will not become exposed or infected,
and cannot rely on long-term studies to predict my result. I am accepting that uncertainty as part of choosing this treatment.
Initial to confirm this was explained to you:
I understand that this is a custom device with limited long-term evidence, that the published studies are small and short, and that
the rate of the gum opening over the framework is substantial.
I understand that no one has told me how many years this device will last, and that no promise or guarantee about its lifespan has
been made to me.
I understand the regulatory status checked in Section 1, including — if it applies to my device — that a custom device is exempt from
the FDA premarket review that mass-produced devices go through.
4. RISKS OF THE SURGERY
Placing this device requires lifting the gum away from the bone over a large area, which makes the surgery longer and the recovery heavier than
for an ordinary implant. No surgery is risk-free, and this list cannot include every possible complication.
•
Common, and usually temporary: significant pain, swelling and bruising of the face and neck, often for a week or more; bleeding and oozing;
stiff jaw and limited opening; sore throat; difficulty eating and speaking for several weeks; numbness of the lip or cheek for hours to days.
•
Less common: infection needing antibiotics, drainage or a second procedure; the wound opening along the incision line; slow healing;
hematoma; damage to the lips, cheeks or tongue; jaw joint pain; scarring; allergic or adverse reaction to a medicine or material, including —
rarely — titanium sensitivity.
•
Uncommon, but serious: nerve injury causing numbness, tingling, burning or pain of the lip, chin, cheek, side of the nose, gums or tongue,
and/or a change in taste. Because the framework is seated over a wide area of bone and may pass close to the mental, inferior alveolar or
infraorbital nerves, this risk is higher than for a single ordinary implant. It usually improves, but it can be permanent; an opening into the
sinus or nose; sinus infection; fracture of a thin, atrophic jaw; infection spreading into the face or neck; heavy bleeding.
•
Rare: medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), more likely with bone-strengthening or anti-cancer drugs or previous radiation
to the jaws; permanent change in facial appearance; life-threatening complications.
5. RISKS SPECIFIC TO A CUSTOM SUBPERIOSTEAL IMPLANT
•
Framework exposure — the most common problem. The gum over the framework can thin, shrink or open, leaving part of the metal visible or
palpable in the mouth. Sometimes this is stable and simply watched; sometimes it needs a gum graft to cover it; and sometimes it leads to
ongoing infection and to removal of the device.
•
Infection travels along the whole device. Because the framework is a single connected structure resting on bone, an infection at one point can
spread along it. Unlike a single failing implant, this often cannot be treated by removing one small part — treatment usually means removing the
entire framework.
•
The device may not fit at surgery. The framework is built from a CT scan taken before surgery. Scan distortion, movement, metal artifact,
changes in the bone between the scan and the operation, or manufacturing tolerance can mean the framework does not seat correctly. If that
happens, my surgeon may have to adjust it, re-scan and re-order a new one, place a different type of implant, or stop and close, leaving me
without the planned treatment that day. A second custom device means a new scan, new fabrication, new surgery and, usually, an additional
fee that may not be refundable.
•
Delay between scan and surgery. Teeth that are extracted, bone that resorbs, or an infection that develops while the device is being made can
change my anatomy enough that the framework no longer fits.
•
Hardware problems. Fixation screws can loosen, break or be lost; an arm of the framework can fracture; the posts that come through the gum
can loosen or fracture. Repairing a custom framework in the mouth is limited, and some failures can only be solved by replacing the whole
device.
•
It does not integrate the way an ordinary implant does. The framework rests on the bone rather than inside it, so it is held mainly by screws
and by the soft tissue seal around the posts. That seal is the known weak point of this design, and keeping it clean is critical.
•
Removal is a bigger operation. If the device must be removed, that is a larger surgery than removing an ordinary implant. Bone may be lost or
reshaped in the process, healing takes longer, and my options afterwards may be fewer and more difficult than the ones I have today —
including the possibility that only a removable denture, on a poorer ridge, remains.
•
Soft tissue quality matters. Thin or mobile gum over the framework raises the risk of exposure, so additional soft tissue grafting may be
recommended at the time of surgery or later, at additional cost.
•
The bridge on top. The prosthesis attached to the device carries the same issues as any full-arch bridge: daily cleaning under it, food and air
passing beneath it, speech changes, chipping and wear, screw loosening, professional removal and cleaning, and eventual replacement at
additional cost. Grinding and clenching increase all of these, and a night guard is usually required.

2. RISKS THAT APPLY TO ANY ORAL SURGERY
No surgery is risk-free, and no result can be promised or guaranteed. The risks below are the ones a reasonable patient would want to know
about. They are grouped by how often they happen. This list cannot include every possible complication.
•
Common, and usually temporary: pain; swelling; bruising; bleeding and oozing for the first day; stiff jaw and limited mouth opening; sore
throat; cracked or sore corners of the mouth; bad taste or odor; nearby teeth feeling loose or sensitive; a small amount of numbness for a few
hours after local anesthetic.
•
Less common: infection needing antibiotics, drainage, or a second procedure; dry socket; slow or incomplete healing; damage to nearby teeth,
fillings, crowns, bridges, dentures or braces; cuts, burns or bruises of the lip, cheek, gum or tongue; jaw joint (TMJ) pain, clicking or locking;
scarring; small pieces of tooth or bone that work their way out later or must be removed; allergic or other adverse reaction to a medicine or
material; a change in how the teeth fit together.
•
Uncommon, but serious: nerve injury — numbness, tingling, burning, or pain in the lip, chin, cheek, gums, teeth or tongue, and/or a change or
loss of taste. This can come from the surgery itself or from the anesthetic injection. It usually improves over weeks to months, but it can last
longer and in some cases is permanent; an opening between the mouth and the sinus or nose that may need a second operation to close; a
tooth, root or implant pushed into the sinus or another space; broken jaw; infection that spreads into the face or neck and requires hospital care;
bleeding heavy enough to need a transfusion; swallowing or breathing in a small instrument or fragment.
•
Rare: medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) — bone that will not heal and stays exposed. The risk is higher if you take or
have ever taken bone-strengthening or anti-cancer drugs such as alendronate (Fosamax), zoledronic acid (Reclast, Zometa), denosumab
(Prolia, Xgeva), or certain targeted therapies, or if you have had radiation to the jaws; permanent change in facial appearance; life-threatening
complications.
Things that make your risk higher. Smoking or vaping, alcohol or recreational drug use, uncontrolled diabetes, steroids or drugs that lower
immunity, blood thinners, previous radiation to the head or neck, and poor oral hygiene all significantly increase the chance of infection, dry
socket, poor healing, and failure of grafts and implants. Tell your surgeon now if any of these apply to you.

3. ADDITIONAL RISKS — these apply only to the procedures checked in Section 1
•
Wisdom teeth, lower molars and coronectomy. These teeth sit closest to the nerve that supplies the lower lip, chin and tongue, so the chance
of numbness is higher than for other teeth. Upper teeth sit against the sinus. In a coronectomy the root is left in place on purpose; it may later
become infected, move toward the surface, or need to be removed in a second procedure.
•
Dental implants. The implant may fail to fuse with the bone, loosen, break, or have to be removed — sometimes months or years later. Bone
and gum can be lost around an implant (peri-implantitis). Your anatomy may make it impossible to place the implant as planned, in the ideal
position, or at all, and the plan may change during surgery. You may see gum recession, metal showing through the gum, an uneven gum line,
or a result you do not find attractive. Screws and crowns can loosen or fracture and need repair or replacement. Implants are not permanent, are
not guaranteed for life, and need cleaning and regular check-ups just like teeth. The crown, bridge or denture that attaches to the implant is
separate treatment with a separate fee, and is often done by another dentist.
•
Bone grafts, membranes and sinus lifts. The graft may become infected, come apart, be partly or completely lost, or not produce enough
bone — in which case grafting may have to be repeated or the plan abandoned. A membrane may become exposed and need removal. In a
sinus lift, the sinus membrane can tear, and you may get sinus congestion, a sinus infection, or graft material moving into the sinus. Grafted
bone can shrink over time.
•
Graft material. Donor and animal-derived grafts are processed, screened and regulated; the chance of passing on an infection is extremely
small but is not zero. Tell us now if you decline donor or animal tissue for personal or religious reasons.
•
Soft tissue grafts (connective tissue, acellular dermal). Pain and bleeding at the donor site on the palate; graft shrinkage or loss; color or
texture that does not match the surrounding gum; incomplete coverage requiring a repeat graft.
•
Biopsy. The tissue removed is sent to a pathology laboratory. A biopsy identifies a lesion but does not by itself treat it, and further surgery or
referral may be needed. Results usually take one to two weeks; we will contact you, and you should call us if you have not heard back.
•
Apicoectomy. Root-end surgery may not save the tooth, and the tooth may still need to be removed later.
•
Frenectomy. The band of tissue can re-form or scar down, and a second procedure is sometimes needed. Speech, feeding or orthodontic
results vary and are not guaranteed.
•
Alveoloplasty, alveolectomy, vestibuloplasty. Reshaping the ridge changes its height and shape, so a denture made before surgery will
usually need relining or remaking, at additional cost.
•
Venipuncture and marrow aspiration. Bruising, pain, swelling, infection, or irritation of a nerve or vein at the site; rarely a blood clot in the vein
or lasting discomfort.
•
Incision and drainage. You may need repeat drainage, a drain left in place for several days, IV antibiotics, or admission to a hospital.
